issues.problem: The station straddles two boroughs; its entrance is in Bexley, only the platforms are in Greenwich. Lesnes Abbey ruins are also in Bexley.
issues.correct: Local authorities: London Borough of Bexley and Royal Borough of Greenwich; entrance in Bexley.

issues.claim: The Saxon name is an early form of Albert
issues.problem: Albert comes from Adalbert, whose Old English form is Æthelbeorht, not Ealhbeorht. Wikipedia does not make the Albert link (only Londonist does, loosely).
issues.correct: Alperton = 'farmstead or estate associated with a man named Ealhbeorht'. Albert's Old English equivalent is Æthelbeorht.
issues.suggested_text: Nothing else is known about him. The station opened in 1903 as Perivale-Alperton and took its present name in 1910.

issues.claim: It was recorded as Berecingas in the 8th century.
issues.problem: Berecingas is the Old English name, but the earliest dated record (a charter of 735) has the form Berecingum. The man's name is given as Bereca, not Berica.
issues.correct: Old English Berecingas, 'followers of Bereca' or 'settlement by the birch trees'; first dated record 735 as Berecingum. Abbey founded 666.
issues.suggested_head: 'Barking' means the people of Bereca, or the settlement by the birch trees.
issues.suggested_text: It was recorded as Berecingum in 735. Barking Abbey, founded in the 7th century, was one of the most important nunneries in England.

issues.claim: It has no known historical source. It was probably meant to sound grand and to pair with Earl's Court, the next station along.
issues.problem: Wikipedia gives a possible source: Baronscourt in County Tyrone, linked to the developer Sir William Palliser. The Earl's Court pairing is Londonist's guess. Also, Earl's Court is the next stop only on the Piccadilly line; on the District line West Kensington lies between.
issues.correct: Name 'possibly inspired by the Baronscourt estate in County Tyrone', where Sir William Palliser may have had connections; Londonist says it was paired with Earl's Court. Station opened 1905.
issues.suggested_text: It may come from Baronscourt in Northern Ireland, linked to the developer Sir William Palliser. It may also be a play on Earl's Court, the next stop on the Piccadilly line.

issues.claim: The Bayard family owned land here
issues.problem: Stated as fact, but the source gives two readings: a watering place for horses ('bayard' = a bay horse) or one belonging to the Bayard family.
issues.correct: 'Bayards Watering Place' (1380) 'meant either a watering place for horses, or the watering place that belonged to the Bayard family.'
issues.suggested_text: 'Bayard' may be a family name, or an old word for a horse. The 'watering' was a place by the River Westbourne where animals drank; the river now flows in a pipe under the streets.

issues.claim: The river wall was made of dark earth.
issues.problem: No source found for the material. Wikipedia says only that the name comes from the colour of the medieval river wall. Checked Wikipedia (Blackwall, London); Jamestown sailing on 20 Dec 1606 is confirmed.
issues.correct: Name 'from the colour of the river wall, built - with its stairs - in the Middle Ages'; material not stated.
issues.suggested_text: The name probably comes from the dark colour of the medieval river wall. Ships sailed from Blackwall in 1606 to found Jamestown in Virginia, the first lasting English colony in America.

issues.claim: who owned land here in the 13th century
issues.problem: Sources disagree on the century: Londonist says 13th century; Hornsey Historical Society says land held by John Le Bounde in the 14th century. Wikipedia mentions only Bounds Green Farm. EPNS page could not be fetched (redirect).
issues.correct: Hornsey Historical Society: 'land held by John Le Bounde in the 14th century'.
issues.suggested_head: Named after the le Bounde family, who held land here in the Middle Ages.

issues.claim: The name suggests a burnt oak tree, but its story is unknown.
issues.problem: Wikipedia gives a story: the 1754 field had an ancient oak burnt by lightning, standing on the Little Stanmore/Kingsbury parish boundary. It is not well sourced, but 'unknown' goes further than the sources. The 1754 Watling Street field record is confirmed.
issues.correct: Name from a field that 'had contained an ancient oak tree', burnt by lightning some time before the 1750s.
issues.suggested_head: Named after an old oak tree, said to have been burnt by lightning.
issues.suggested_text: The name first appears in 1754 for a field beside Watling Street, the old Roman road. The oak itself is long gone.

issues.claim: Named after Bush Hill, an old name for the high ground here.
issues.problem: No source found saying Bush Hill was a name for high ground. Hidden London says the suburb took the name of the Bush Hill Park estate, dating from 1671, with a mansion by 1724. Estate building from 1877 (houses 1880-86) and station of 1880 are confirmed.
issues.correct: Bush Hill Park was an estate (from 1671) with a brick mansion; the Bush Hill Park Company built houses from 1877; station opened 1880.
issues.suggested_head: Named after Bush Hill Park, an old country estate with a mansion.

issues.claim: It comes from Old English box, box tree, and hæg, an enclosure.
issues.problem: Stated as fact, but Wikipedia gives a different first element: bysc, 'bush, thicket', so 'enclosure made of bushes'. The box-tree reading is one of two theories.
issues.correct: Wikipedia: compound of Old English bysc ('bush, thicket') and hæg ('enclosure'). Station location in Oxhey (Borough of Watford) confirmed.
issues.suggested_head: 'Bushey' means an enclosure made of bushes, or one near box trees.
issues.suggested_text: The second part is Old English hæg, an enclosure; the first may be bysc, bush, or box, box tree. The station is actually in Oxhey, on the Watford side.
